name: Software Architecture Foundations
tagline: From requirements to a documented, defensible design.
description: Start here if architecture is new to you. You will learn what architecture actually is, how to gather requirements and quality goals, how the classic styles differ, and how to draw and document a design other people can build from. No distributed-systems background needed.
outcomes: Explain the difference between architecture, design and implementation.
Turn business requirements into quality attributes you can test.
Choose between layered, monolith, service-based and microservice styles.
Draw a system context, container and sequence diagram that a stranger can read.
Write an architecture decision record that records the trade-off, not just the outcome.

steps.why: The vocabulary: scalability, reliability, maintainability, consistency, and the blueprint questions every design must answer.
What the backend actually consists of — servers, APIs, data, auth, queues — before you start splitting it.
Requirements analysis and architecture evaluation (ATAM/SAAM), so decisions are tested against goals.
The design trade-offs: consistency vs latency, dynamic load balancing, monitoring from day one.
Diagram types and when each one earns its place.
Practise the C4 levels and write a real ADR for a design you have seen.
Keeping documentation alive across sprints instead of letting it rot.

name: Distributed Systems Engineer
tagline: Consistency, caches, retries and failure — with the arithmetic.
description: The engineering core. You will reason about CAP and PACELC without hand-waving, size a quorum, compute whether a cache is worth it, and make a service survive a dependency that has stopped answering.
outcomes: Place a design on the CAP and PACELC axes and justify the choice.
Compute read/write quorum sizes and explain the failure each one tolerates.
Estimate cache hit ratio, latency and the cost of a stampede.
Design timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers and fallbacks that fail safely.
State an RPO/RTO target and derive a backup and restore plan from it.

steps.why: Nodes, partitioning, failover and the consistency spectrum.
The worked arithmetic behind CAP, quorums and read-your-writes.
The pattern catalogue: ambassador, circuit breaker, CQRS, event sourcing.
Build the failure handling: budgets, backoff maths, breaker states, bulkheads.
Trade-off vocabulary and the caching chapter, at book depth. Large — read in two sittings.
Hit-ratio maths, eviction, invalidation and stampede control.
Turn an availability promise into concrete backup frequency and a tested restore.
What actually happens when a whole cloud region degrades.

name: Microservices Practitioner
tagline: Split a system without building a distributed monolith.
description: Microservices fail in predictable ways: wrong boundaries, shared databases, synchronous chains, unclear ownership. This path is about drawing the lines in the right place and keeping them.
outcomes: Derive service boundaries from business capabilities rather than technical layers.
Decide between choreography and orchestration for a given flow.
Design a read model and an event log that can be replayed.
Keep a service's data private and still answer cross-service queries.
Explain the cost of a service you do not split.

steps.why: The pattern, its benefits, and its real costs.
Why monoliths hurt, with Walmart and Netflix as evidence.
The anti-pattern checklist: distributed monolith, shared ownership, missing fallbacks.
API flow diagrams as the contract between teams.
Separate reads from writes and rebuild state from an event log.
Give each service its own schema — and prove it with constraints and roles.
How the data layer has to change when the app is distributed.

name: Data & Resilience Engineer
tagline: Schemas, indexes, regions, backups and failure drills.
description: The database is where architecture becomes irreversible. This path covers modelling, distributed SQL behaviour, tuning, TTL, backups, and the difference between high availability and disaster recovery.
outcomes: Model entities and relationships, then enforce them with constraints.
Read an execution plan and choose indexes deliberately.
Place data regionally and explain the latency and compliance consequences.
Use TTL and partitioning to keep hot tables small.
Distinguish HA from DR and design a restore you have actually rehearsed.

steps.why: Constraints as the first line of data quality.
Worked schema: keys, checks, indexes and row-level access.
How a distributed SQL database keeps ACID while scaling writes.
Seven tuning levers, from partial indexes to admission control.
Row-level TTL and partition staggering under game-scale ingestion.
Managed vs customer-managed backups and point-in-time restore windows.
RPO/RTO, off-site storage, and whole-cluster loss.
Write the plan and run the drill against real numbers.
Eleven failure modes and how a resilient cluster absorbs them.

name: Multiplayer Backend Engineer
tagline: Netcode, sessions, matchmaking and game-scale data.
description: A multiplayer game is a distributed system with a 50 ms deadline. This path follows the request path: client prediction, authoritative simulation, session placement, matchmaking, and the storage that survives a live-ops event.
outcomes: Explain what the client may predict and what only the server may decide.
Size a tick rate and bandwidth budget for a given genre.
Design a matchmaking loop with tickets, pools and a match function.
Place game servers for latency and choose a session model.
Expire and partition short-lived game data without hurting peak load.

steps.why: Map each backend concern to a tool, so the rest of the path has names.
Client-server, peer-to-peer and hybrid, chosen by genre and tolerance for cheating.
Authoritative servers, client prediction and reconciliation.
The tick loop with real numbers: input delay, correction, interpolation, bandwidth.
Why the hot path stays in memory and why server placement is physics.
Shared services, entitlements and multi-region data locality.
Tickets, profiles, Director and the match function.
Design the pools, the quality function and the latency budget end to end.
TTL and regional rows for MMORPG-scale writes.
Game loop, command pattern and decoupling — the code-level view.

name: Architecture Communication & EA
tagline: Make the design legible to engineers, executives and auditors.
description: An architecture nobody can read is an architecture nobody follows. This path covers diagram craft, API flows, enterprise strategy, decision records, and keeping documentation current inside an agile process.
outcomes: Pick the diagram that answers the question being asked.
Apply layout, notation and accessibility rules so a diagram survives review.
Connect business goals to technology choices in an enterprise context.
Record decisions as ADRs and keep them versioned.
Fit documentation work into sprint 0, planning, review and retrospective.

steps.why: System, sequence and network diagrams: purpose and parts.
Standard microservice components and the notation that goes with them.
API flow diagrams as executable-looking contracts.
Draw the four C4 levels and write the decision record behind them.
Enterprise architecture: aligning technology with business goals.
Documentation as a maintained activity, not a deliverable.
Process orchestration across IT and business — the EA view of workflows.
